questions.domain: Statistics & Probability: Making Inferences & Justifying Conclusions
questions.skill: Evaluate the conclusions of reports based on data
questions.standard_level: Probability & Statistics. Common Core groups high-school standards by category, not by course; this bank places this one in Probability & Statistics, following the Common Core traditional pathway (Appendix A) except where engine/hs_courses.py says otherwise.
questions.prompt: A report says: "Teens who eat breakfast get better grades, so eating breakfast raises grades." The data came from a survey of 2,000 randomly chosen teens. What is the main problem?
questions.prompt_markup: A report says: "Teens who eat breakfast get better grades, so eating breakfast raises grades." The data came from a survey of 2,000 randomly chosen teens. What is the main problem?

choices.text: A survey shows association, not that breakfast causes better grades.
A random sample of 2,000 teens is far too small for any survey.
Grades cannot be compared between different groups of teens.
Random samples cannot be used to describe a population of teens.

questions.correct_answer: A survey shows association, not that breakfast causes better grades.

Three thousand replies is too few to report.

questions.correct_answer: Readers chose to reply, so the sample is likely biased.

questions.prompt: A randomized experiment found that a reading program raised scores of 3rd graders in one district. Which conclusion is best supported?
questions.prompt_markup: A randomized experiment found that a reading program raised scores of 3rd graders in one district. Which conclusion is best supported?

choices.text: The program will raise scores for students of every age everywhere.
The program caused higher scores for students like those in the study.
The program is associated with scores but did not cause any change.
Nothing can be concluded, because only one district was studied.

questions.correct_answer: The program caused higher scores for students like those in the study.
questions.grading_note: Cause for the subjects; limited generalization.

questions.prompt: A report on 12 patients says a new treatment "works for everyone," because 9 of the 12 improved. Which criticism is most important?
questions.prompt_markup: A report on 12 patients says a new treatment "works for everyone," because 9 of the 12 improved. Which criticism is most important?

choices.text: Twelve patients is too many to study at once.

No comparison group, and 3 of the 12 did not improve.
Improvement cannot be measured in patients.

questions.grading_note: No control; and "everyone" contradicts the data.

sections.skill: Know what each design can support

sections.skill: Weigh several flaws and decide what a report shows

branch.new_demand: Combine design, bias and scope to decide what a report actually shows.
branch.builds_on: Builds on FORWARD 1: after naming individual biases, the student weighs them together.

questions.domain: Statistics & Probability: Making Inferences & Justifying Conclusions
questions.skill: Weigh several flaws and decide what a report shows

questions.prompt: An app maker reports: "Users who used our app for 30 days lost 8 pounds on average." The users were volunteers and there was no comparison group. Which conclusion is justified?
questions.prompt_markup: An app maker reports: "Users who used our app for 30 days lost 8 pounds on average." The users were volunteers and there was no comparison group. Which conclusion is justified?

choices.text: Only that these volunteers lost weight; the app's role is unclear.
The app causes weight loss in everyone who uses it.
Every single user of the app lost exactly 8 pounds.
The study has shown that the app has no effect on weight.

questions.correct_answer: Only that these volunteers lost weight; the app's role is unclear.
